title: 07. Advanced & Agentic RAG: MCP Transport Layers (How Messages Travel)
summary: In the last lesson we learned the exact shape of JSON-RPC messages. Today we learn how those messages actually travel between the client and the server.
objectives: ① Real-World Analogy — The Post Office

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: **In the last lesson** we learned the exact shape of JSON-RPC messages. **Today** we learn how those messages actually travel between the client and the server.

sections.title: ① Real-World Analogy — The Post Office
sections.body:
Imagine you have written a letter (the JSON-RPC message). Now you need to **send** it. You have options:

1. **Hand it directly** to the person (they are standing right next to you)
2. **Mail it** through the postal service (they are in another city)

The letter is the same either way. The **transport** is just the delivery method.

MCP has two transport options:
- **stdio** = hand delivery (person is right next to you — on the same computer)
- **HTTP + SSE** = postal service (person might be anywhere — on the internet)

sections.title: ② Plain English Explanation
sections.body:
A **transport layer** is just the mechanism that moves JSON-RPC messages from point A to point B. The messages are always the same JSON structure — only the delivery method changes.

MCP currently has two standard transports:

1. **stdio (Standard Input/Output):** Messages are sent through the terminal's input and output streams. This is how your keyboard and screen work — `stdin` is your keyboard, `stdout` is your screen. MCP hijacks these to send structured messages instead.

2. **HTTP + SSE (Server-Sent Events):** Messages go over the network like a website. The client sends HTTP POST requests to the server. The server streams back responses using SSE (a web technology for one-way streaming).

sections.title: ③ Why Does This Matter?
sections.body: Choosing the wrong transport is a common beginner mistake that leads to frustrating bugs. Use **stdio** when your server runs on the same machine as the client (the most common case when starting out). Use **HTTP** when your server needs to be reachable over a network (for cloud deployments or shared tools).

sections.title: ④ Step-by-Step Technical Explanation
sections.body:
### Transport 1: stdio

```
How stdio works:

Your MCP Server (my_server.py)
  └── When launched, it reads JSON-RPC messages from stdin (standard input)
  └── It writes JSON-RPC responses to stdout (standard output)

The MCP Client (Claude Desktop, your Python client, etc.)
  └── It launches your server as a SUBPROCESS (like running a Python script)
  └── It sends JSON-RPC messages by writing to the server's stdin
  └── It reads responses from the server's stdout
```

Think of it like two programs passing notes through a shared pipe.

```
CLIENT PROCESS                    SERVER PROCESS (my_server.py)
─────────────────                 ─────────────────────────────
writes to server's stdin ──────►  reads from stdin
                                  processes the request
reads from server's stdout ◄────  writes to stdout
```

**When to use stdio:**
- Local development and testing (almost always)
- Command-line tools
- Tools that run on the user's own machine
- Tools used with Claude Desktop (it always uses stdio)

### Transport 2: HTTP + SSE

```
How HTTP+SSE works:

Your MCP Server runs as a web server (like a Flask app)
  └── Client sends requests via HTTP POST to /messages endpoint
  └── Server streams back responses using SSE (Server-Sent Events)
  └── Initial connection uses a /sse endpoint for setup

SSE (Server-Sent Events):
  └── A web standard for "push" communication
  └── Server can keep a connection open and push data
  └── One-directional: only server pushes to client
  └── Client uses HTTP POST to send messages TO the server
```

**When to use HTTP:**
- Your server needs to be accessed from the internet
- Multiple clients need to connect to the same server
- You are deploying to a cloud service
- Your server needs to be always-on (not launched as a subprocess)

sections.title: ⑤ Beginner-Friendly Code Example
sections.body:
Let us build the **same simple server** and show how to run it on **both** transports. We will use the FastMCP library here (we will learn it in depth in Lesson 8 — for now just notice the transport switching).

```python
# simple_server.py
# A minimal MCP server that can run on EITHER stdio OR http
# Run this file after: pip install fastmcp

from fastmcp import FastMCP   # Import the FastMCP library

# Create our MCP server — give it a name (any name you like)
mcp = FastMCP("My First Server")

# Register a tool called "greet"
# The @mcp.tool() decorator tells FastMCP: "this function is a tool"
@mcp.tool()
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    """
    Say hello to someone.
    name: The name of the person to greet
    """
    return f"Hello, {name}! Welcome to MCP!"   # Return the greeting

# ─── HOW TO RUN ON DIFFERENT TRANSPORTS ──────────────────────────────

# To run with STDIO transport (default — for local use):
# python simple_server.py
# OR explicitly:
# mcp.run(transport="stdio")

# To run with HTTP+SSE transport (for network access):
# mcp.run(transport="sse", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
# Then visit: http://localhost:8000/sse

# The main block — this runs when you execute the file directly
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Run with stdio by default
    # The server will wait for JSON-RPC messages on stdin
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")   # Change "stdio" to "sse" for HTTP mode
```

Now let us write a separate file that shows **how to tell the difference** when choosing:

```python
# choose_transport.py
# This is a guide to help you decide which transport to use
# Run this to see the decision logic: python choose_transport.py

def choose_transport(scenario: str) -> str:
    """
    Given a scenario, return which MCP transport to use.
    """
    scenarios = {
        "testing locally":              "stdio  ← always use this for local dev",
        "claude desktop integration":   "stdio  ← Claude Desktop only supports stdio",
        "deployed to AWS/GCP/Azure":    "http   ← must be reachable over network",
        "multiple users sharing tools": "http   ← many clients, one server",
        "CLI tool":                     "stdio  ← running locally from terminal",
        "always-on server":             "http   ← needs to stay running 24/7",
    }
    return scenarios.get(scenario, "stdio  ← default to stdio when unsure")

# Print the transport guide
print("=" * 55)
print("MCP TRANSPORT DECISION GUIDE")
print("=" * 55)

test_scenarios = [
    "testing locally",
    "claude desktop integration",
    "deployed to AWS/GCP/Azure",
    "multiple users sharing tools",
    "CLI tool",
    "always-on server",
]

for scenario in test_scenarios:
    transport = choose_transport(scenario)
    print(f"\n📍 Scenario: {scenario}")
    print(f"   Use:      {transport}")

print("\n" + "=" * 55)
print("BOTTOM LINE: Start with stdio. Switch to HTTP only when you")
print("need remote access or multiple simultaneous clients.")
print("=" * 55)
```

**Expected Output:**

```
=======================================================
MCP TRANSPORT DECISION GUIDE
=======================================================

📍 Scenario: testing locally
   Use:      stdio  ← always use this for local dev

📍 Scenario: claude desktop integration
   Use:      stdio  ← Claude Desktop only supports stdio

📍 Scenario: deployed to AWS/GCP/Azure
   Use:      http   ← must be reachable over network

📍 Scenario: multiple users sharing tools
   Use:      http   ← many clients, one server

📍 Scenario: CLI tool
   Use:      stdio  ← running locally from terminal

📍 Scenario: always-on server
   Use:      http   ← needs to stay running 24/7

=======================================================
BOTTOM LINE: Start with stdio. Switch to HTTP only when you
need remote access or multiple simultaneous clients.
=======================================================
```

sections.title: ⑥ Common Beginner Mistakes
sections.body:
```
❌ Mistake 1: Printing debug messages to stdout in a stdio server
   Why it happens: Developers naturally use print() for debugging
   ✅ Fix: In stdio mode, stdout is RESERVED for MCP messages.
         Use print(..., file=sys.stderr) or use the logging module.
         Any stray print() will corrupt the MCP message stream.

❌ Mistake 2: Using HTTP transport for Claude Desktop
   Why it happens: Developer deploys server to cloud, expects Claude to find it
   ✅ Fix: Claude Desktop ONLY supports stdio (as of 2024).
         Use stdio for Claude Desktop. HTTP is for other clients.

❌ Mistake 3: Forgetting to install the server as a subprocess in stdio mode
   Why it happens: Thinking the server needs to already be running
   ✅ Fix: In stdio mode, the CLIENT launches the server automatically.
         The server does NOT need to be pre-running. The client starts it.

❌ Mistake 4: Trying to run stdio server on port 8000
   Why it happens: Confusion between stdio and http transports
   ✅ Fix: stdio servers have NO port. They communicate through pipes.
         Only HTTP servers have a port number.

❌ Mistake 5: Not handling server crashes in production HTTP mode
   Why it happens: stdio mode auto-restarts when client reconnects
   ✅ Fix: HTTP servers need a process manager (systemd, supervisor,
         or Docker restart policy) to auto-restart on crash.
```

sections.title: ⑦ Quick Recap — What Did We Just Learn?
sections.body:
- ✅ Transport = how JSON-RPC messages physically travel between client and server
- ✅ **stdio** = same machine, server is launched as subprocess, no port needed
- ✅ **HTTP+SSE** = over network, server runs independently, has a URL/port
- ✅ **Default choice:** always start with stdio — simpler, no networking needed
- ✅ Never use `print()` in a stdio server — it breaks the message stream!
